text: Most Canadians will never set foot in the top half of British Columbia. And honestly, most of them couldn't tell you what's up there. A town that was built brand new, with a hospital, a shopping mall and a swimming pool, and then emptied out in about eighteen months. It's still standing there today, lights off, waiting. A volcano that erupted about three hundred years ago and buried whole villages under lava. A river that was turned around and sent backwards through a mountain. A road the American army built in eight months during the war. And a stretch of wild country so big and so empty that you could drop a few European countries into it and nobody would notice.

I'm Gordie. I flew bush planes over this country for forty years, and before that I surveyed a good chunk of it on foot. I've landed on lakes up there that don't have names on most maps. So pull up a chair, because today I'm going to take you through northern British Columbia, piece by piece, and show you what's hiding up there. Some of it is beautiful. Some of it is a little frightening. And some of it, I still can't fully explain.
Let's start with the map, because the map itself is the first secret.

British Columbia is huge. It's bigger than France and Germany put together. But when most people picture B.C., they picture Vancouver, Victoria, maybe Whistler, maybe the Okanagan with its vineyards and lakes. All of that sits in the bottom corner. Now draw a line across the province around Prince George, roughly in the middle. Everything above that line is what we call the North. That's well over half of the province. And the number of people living up there? Only around one in twenty British Columbians. Picture it like this. You take a country the size of a big European nation, and you put the population of one medium-sized city across all of it. That's northern B.C.

When I first flew up there as a young man, an older pilot told me something I never forgot. He said, Gordie, down south they measure distance in kilometres. Up here we measure it in hours, and in how much fuel you've got left. He wasn't joking. There are places up there where, if your engine quits, the nearest road might be two hundred kilometres away, and the nearest person might be further than that.

And yet this empty land has quietly shaped the whole country. The gold that started towns, the power that runs factories, the port that ships grain to Asia, the jade in shops around the world. A lot of it comes out of the North. Most people just never connect the dots.
So let's connect them. We'll go from east to west, from the Alaska Highway all the way out to the islands at the edge of the Pacific.

Our first stop is a little town called Dawson Creek, right up against the Alberta border. In the middle of town there's a post with a sign on it that says Mile Zero. That's where the Alaska Highway begins.

Here's the story behind that sign, and it's a wild one. In December of nineteen forty-one, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor. Suddenly the Americans were terrified that Alaska could be invaded, and there was no road to get there. None. Alaska was cut off by thousands of kilometres of mountains, muskeg and forest, most of it right here in northern British Columbia and the Yukon.

So in early nineteen forty-two, the United States Army sent in thousands of soldiers, with bulldozers and trucks, and told them to punch a road through to Alaska. Around ten thousand troops worked on it, and a lot of them had never seen a winter like that in their lives. They worked through mosquitoes so thick you couldn't see your own hands, and later through temperatures that froze the oil in their machines. Many of the soldiers on the hardest stretches were Black regiments, who weren't given the credit they deserved for decades.

And here's the part that still amazes me. They finished a rough road, more than two thousand seven hundred kilometres long, in about eight months. Eight months. Today it takes longer than that to fix one bridge in some cities.

The road they built was rough, a winding track that followed the easiest ground, not the straightest line. Over the years it has been straightened and paved, and today it's a real highway. But when you drive it, you can still feel how wild it is. You'll see bison standing on the shoulder like they own the place, because frankly, they do. You'll see stone sheep licking salt off the road. And you'll drive for an hour without passing another car.
But before we head up that highway, I want to take you on a little detour south of Dawson Creek, into the foothills. Because there's a town down there with a secret that two kids found by accident.

The town is called Tumbler Ridge. It's young, as towns go. It was built in the early nineteen-eighties, almost from scratch, for the coal mines in the hills around it. Streets, houses, a school, all laid out at once in the middle of the forest.

Then, in the summer of two thousand, two boys were floating down a creek near town on inner tubes. And one of them noticed something strange in the rock along the bank. Big shapes, pressed into the stone, one after another. Like giant footprints.

That's exactly what they were. Dinosaur footprints. The boys told their parents, the parents called the experts, and when the scientists came up and started looking, they found more. And more. Trackways of dinosaurs that walked across these mud flats tens of millions of years ago, when this whole country looked completely different. Later they found bones too, some of the first dinosaur bones ever found in British Columbia.

I love this story, because it's so northern. Nobody went looking. It took two kids on inner tubes, in a creek most people would never visit, to find a whole lost world that had been sitting there the entire time.

Today the whole area is recognized as a UNESCO Global Geopark, one of only a handful in North America. There's a little research centre in town with the tracks and bones, and if you go in the right season, you can walk out with a guide and see footprints in the rock with your own eyes. You put your hand inside one, and it's bigger than your hand. And you think, something stood right here.
Okay. Back to the highway.

Up the highway, past Fort Nelson, the road climbs into the northern Rockies. And there, beside a little river, there's something you would not expect to find in a land of snow and ice. Hot springs. The Liard River Hot Springs. Steaming water, coming straight up out of the ground, warm as a bath, in the middle of the boreal forest. Because the water stays warm all winter, the plants around it grow differently from everything else for miles. There are ferns and orchids there that you'd expect much further south. Soldiers building the highway found these springs in nineteen forty-two and thought they'd walked into paradise. I can tell you, after a long cold day of flying, sitting in that water with snow falling on your head is about as close to heaven as I've been.
Now, right around there, look west on the map, and you'll see a huge area with almost no roads at all. That's the Muskwa-Kechika. And this is one of the real secrets of northern B.C.

The Muskwa-Kechika is a protected management area of around six million hectares. To give you a sense of that, it's bigger than many entire countries. And inside it, there are no towns. No paved roads. Just mountains, valleys, rivers and animals. People who study wildlife sometimes call it the Serengeti of the North, because of how many large animals still roam free there. Stone sheep, mountain goats, elk, moose, caribou, wolves, grizzly bears. In most of the world, those big animals were pushed out long ago. Here they never left.

I've flown over the Muskwa-Kechika at low level, and it does something to you. You fly for an hour, and there is no sign of a human being. No power line, no cabin, no road. Just a river shining in the sun and a herd of caribou running from the sound of your engine. You realize that this is what most of North America looked like before any of us got here. And you realize how lucky we are that one piece of it is still left.

Now, if you keep heading northwest, right up against the Yukon border, there's a little town on the shore of a giant lake. The lake is Atlin Lake, the biggest natural lake in British Columbia. And the town is Atlin.

In eighteen ninety-eight, everybody in the world was talking about the Klondike gold rush up in the Yukon. Tens of thousands of people were struggling north to get rich. And two prospectors, coming through this country on their way, decided to try a creek near Atlin Lake. They found gold. Real gold, in the gravel of a little stream called Pine Creek.

Word got out the way it always does. And within months, thousands of people who'd been heading for the Klondike turned around and poured into Atlin instead. A tent city grew up on the shore of the lake almost overnight. There were hotels, stores, saloons, a newspaper, all shipped in over the mountains or across the lakes. For a few years, this remote corner of B.C. was one of the busiest places in the North.

The rush faded, as they always do. But Atlin never quite died. A few hundred people still live there today, in one of the most beautiful settings I've ever seen. Old wooden buildings from the gold rush days still stand on the main street. And out on the creeks, some people are still working for gold, more than a century later. I've landed a float plane on Atlin Lake on a still summer morning, with the mountains and the glaciers reflected so perfectly in the water that you couldn't tell which way was up. Some of the old-timers there will tell you the real gold in Atlin was never in the creeks. It was the place itself.

And here's another piece of history from that same rush that almost nobody remembers. When the gold fever hit, the government needed a way to talk to the Yukon. There was no road, no railway into the interior, no radio. So they built a telegraph line. Just a single wire, strung on poles and trees, across more than a thousand kilometres of the wildest country in North America. It was called the Yukon Telegraph, and it was finished around nineteen-oh-one.

To keep that wire working, the government put men in little log cabins along the line, spaced out every so often through the bush. Two men to a cabin, usually. Their job was to walk the line, find the breaks, and fix them, summer and winter. Some of those operators went months without seeing another living soul except the man they shared the cabin with. They got their supplies once a year. The loneliness drove some of them half crazy. There are stories of men who stopped speaking to each other for an entire winter, and only talked through the telegraph key, to men a hundred kilometres away.

Eventually radio came along, and the line wasn't needed anymore. The cabins were left to the bush. Today, if you know where to look, you can still find the old trail, and here and there a rotting cabin, or a piece of wire wrapped around a tree, or a glass insulator lying in the moss. Little pieces of a lonely job that kept the North connected to the rest of the world.
Now, before we leave that corner of the province, there's one more road I have to tell you about, because it's the road I'd pick if I could only drive one.

It's Highway thirty-seven, the Stewart-Cassiar Highway. It runs north from the Skeena River country, more than eight hundred kilometres, up through the mountains, all the way to the Alaska Highway near the Yukon border. And for most of that distance, there's almost nothing. A few tiny communities. A gas station here and there, sometimes a very long way apart. For years, long stretches of it were gravel, and in a couple of places the road even doubled as an airstrip, so you'd see a sign telling you to watch for planes.

When you drive it, you understand how big this country really is. You go around a bend, and there's a lake nobody has ever bothered to put on a postcard. You go over a pass, and there's a valley full of nothing but trees and river, all the way to the horizon. You see moose, you see black bears, and if you're lucky, a grizzly digging for roots on the side of the road.

And at night, up there, if the sky is clear, you get the show. The northern lights. Green curtains rolling across the whole sky, sometimes with a bit of pink at the edges, moving like they're alive. I've seen them from the cockpit, I've seen them from a tent, and I've seen them standing next to my truck on that highway at two in the morning. You never get used to it. Down south, the city lights wash them out. Up here, there's nothing between you and them.
So if you ever want to see the real North, skip the airport. Take that road.
So that's the wild side, and a bit of the lonely side. But the North also has a side that's man-made, and some of it is enormous.

Head south and west from the Alaska Highway and you'll come to the Peace River country. In the nineteen-sixties, the province built a giant dam on the Peace River, the W.A.C. Bennett Dam. When they closed the gates, the water backed up and created a lake so big it's hard to believe it's not natural. Williston Lake. It's the biggest body of fresh water in British Columbia.

But that lake came at a price, and this is one of the things most Canadians never hear about. Before the water came, there were valleys there. Trapping lines, homes, trails, and a small settlement called Finlay Forks, where two rivers met. The people of the Tsay Keh Dene and other First Nations had lived and hunted in those valleys for generations. When the water rose, all of it went under. Whole valleys, gone. Even today, pilots flying over the lake on a calm day sometimes talk about seeing the tops of drowned trees sticking up through the surface, like the fingers of a forest that never got the chance to leave.

And here's the strange thing about that lake. Because it drowned so much forest, for years afterwards giant mats of floating logs and debris drifted around on it. Boaters had to watch out for them like icebergs. The wind can whip up waves there big enough to sink a boat, because it's so long and narrow. It looks peaceful from the air, but locals give it a lot of respect.
And the Peace River story isn't over. Not by a long shot.

Downstream from the Bennett Dam, the province went back to the same river and built more. A second dam came in the nineteen-eighties. And then, just a few years ago, a third one, the biggest argument in the North in a generation. It's called Site C.

Site C sits on the Peace River not far from Fort St. John. Construction started in twenty fifteen, and it took the better part of ten years and a lot more money than anybody first promised. When it filled, the reservoir backed up along the river for more than eighty kilometres, and it flooded some of the best farmland in the whole North. River bottom land, warm and sheltered, where families had grown vegetables for generations in a part of Canada where most places can barely grow a potato.

Treaty Eight First Nations fought it in the courts for years. They said this valley was where they hunted, fished and buried their people, and that their treaty promised them they could keep doing that. Farmers fought it too. People who'd never agreed on anything stood on the same side of the river for once.

The province said British Columbia needed the power, clean power, for decades to come. And the power is flowing now. But if you ask people in the Peace country, a lot of them will tell you the same thing. Down south, you flip a switch and the lights come on. Up here, people gave up a valley to make that happen. And most of the folks flipping the switch will never know it was there.
Let's keep going west, deeper into the mountains, because now we're getting to the part of this story that I find truly spooky.

Up in the Cassiar country, near the Yukon border, there used to be a town called Cassiar. It was a company town, built around one of the world's important asbestos mines. In its day, it had houses, a school, a hospital, a curling rink, the whole works. Families lived there, kids grew up there, people got married there.

Then the world found out what asbestos does to human lungs. Demand collapsed. The mine closed in the early nineteen-nineties. And within a short time, the whole town was gone. Not abandoned, mind you. Gone. Buildings were sold off and hauled away on trucks, and much of what was left was taken down. If you go there today, you'll find roads leading to nowhere, concrete pads where houses used to be, and big grey piles of tailings on the mountainside. That's it. A whole town, erased from the map, while most of the country never even knew it existed.

But not far from there, there's a little place called Jade City. And this is one of those things that sounds made up, but it's true. The mountains in that area hold huge deposits of nephrite jade, the beautiful deep green stone that people carve into jewellery and sculptures. A lot of the world's nephrite jade has come out of northern British Columbia. Boulders of it, some weighing many tonnes, have been pulled out of those hills and shipped to buyers on the other side of the planet. So the next time you see a green jade carving in a shop somewhere, there's a real chance it started life in a remote valley in northern B.C. where hardly anyone lives.

From there, a long gravel road winds west to one of the most remote settlements in the province, a little place called Telegraph Creek, on the Stikine River. And between here and there, the Stikine does something that very few people have ever seen with their own eyes.

The river cuts through a canyon so deep and so narrow that it's often called the Grand Canyon of the Stikine. The walls rise straight up for hundreds of metres in places, and at the bottom the whole river squeezes through gaps you'd swear were too small for it. The water down there is so violent that the canyon is considered one of the hardest stretches of whitewater on the planet. Only a handful of the world's very best paddlers have ever made it through, and some people call it the Everest of whitewater. For most of human history, nobody could travel through that canyon at all.

Telegraph Creek itself is a story. During the gold rushes of the late eighteen hundreds, paddlewheel steamboats used to come up the Stikine from the coast in Alaska, carrying miners and supplies as far as the river would let them. That's how this little settlement grew. The Tahltan people have lived in this country for thousands of years, and their villages and fishing camps along the river are much older than any steamboat. Some of the old buildings from the steamboat days are still standing in Telegraph Creek, looking out over the river, as if the next boat might come around the bend any minute.

Getting there is half the adventure. The road into Telegraph Creek runs along the edge of a lava canyon, with grades so steep and drop-offs so sheer that people who drive it once usually tell the story for the rest of their lives. I know a fellow who drove it in a rented car and swore he'd never complain about a Vancouver traffic jam again.
Now, if Cassiar was a town that vanished, the next place is even stranger. Because it's a town that never got the chance to live at all.

Go out toward the coast, to the head of a long fjord called Alice Arm, and you'll find a place called Kitsault. In the late nineteen-seventies, a mining company decided to open a big molybdenum mine there. Molybdenum is a metal used to harden steel, and back then the price was high. So the company built a whole brand new town for its workers. And I mean a proper town. Modern houses and apartment buildings. A shopping centre. A swimming pool. A hospital. A library. A pub. Tennis courts. Everything a family could want, in the middle of the coastal wilderness.
Around twelve hundred people moved in. Kids started school. Families planted gardens.

And then, in the early nineteen-eighties, the price of molybdenum crashed. The mine was no longer worth running. And just like that, the whole town was told to pack up and leave. It had been open for only about a year and a half.

Here's the eerie part. Unlike Cassiar, Kitsault wasn't torn down. The company kept it. They kept the heat on in some buildings so the pipes wouldn't freeze, and a caretaker looked after the place for years. So the town just sat there. Furnished. Dishes in cupboards. Books on library shelves. Carpets on the floors. A complete, modern town with no one in it, at the end of a fjord, for decades. People who visited described it like walking through a movie set after the actors went home.

Years later, the whole town was bought by a single private owner, for a few million dollars. Think about that. An entire town, with houses and apartments and a mall, for less than the price of a nice house in Vancouver. There have been ideas over the years about turning it into a retreat, or a place for artists, or an energy project. But as of now, it's mostly still sitting there, quiet, waiting for a purpose.

I flew over Kitsault once, years ago, on a grey afternoon with low cloud. And I'll be honest with you. Seeing all those neat rows of houses with no smoke, no cars, no people. It gave me a chill I can still feel.
Now let's talk about something even older, and a lot more dangerous.

Northern British Columbia is volcano country. Most Canadians don't think of Canada as having volcanoes at all. But up in the northwest part of the province there's a whole field of them. There's a huge volcanic complex called Mount Edziza, with lava flows and cinder cones spread across a high plateau, so colourful in places it looks like someone spilled paint over the mountains. And there are many more scattered through the region.
And one of them, not that long ago, took a terrible toll.

In the Nass Valley, in the territory of the Nisga'a Nation, there's a small volcanic cone called the Tseax Cone. Around three hundred years ago, maybe a little less, it erupted. Lava poured down the valley, flowing for many kilometres and filling the river valley floor. According to Nisga'a oral history, the eruption destroyed villages, and as many as two thousand people lost their lives. Many of them may have been killed not by the lava itself, but by poisonous volcanic gases that settled in the valley.
If those numbers are right, that eruption is considered one of the deadliest natural disasters in what is now Canada. And yet, how many Canadians have ever heard of it? I'd bet almost none.

Today you can drive through the Nisga'a Memorial Lava Bed Park, and it's like driving across the surface of another planet. Black, broken rock as far as you can see, with a thin coat of pale green moss and lichen slowly creeping over it. The river has had to carve a new path. And the Nisga'a people have kept the memory of that day alive through their stories, passed down for generations, as a warning about respecting the land and the creatures that live on it.

When I stood on that lava bed for the first time, it was dead quiet. No birds. Just the wind going over the rock. And I remember thinking, this is not ancient history. This happened around the time my own great-great-grandparents were alive. The ground up there is not finished moving.
And there's something else that happened in the Nass Valley that I think every Canadian should know about, and most don't.

For a very long time, the Nisga'a people asked the government to recognize that this was their land. They'd been asking since the eighteen hundreds. Back then, a group of their chiefs even travelled down to Victoria to make their case. They were turned away. For generations, they kept at it.

And finally, in the year two thousand, it happened. The Nisga'a Treaty came into effect. It was the first modern treaty in British Columbia. It recognized Nisga'a ownership of about two thousand square kilometres of land in the Nass Valley, and their right to govern themselves, with their own government making their own laws on that land. More than a hundred years of asking, and they never gave up.

Just to the east of there, along the Skeena River, there's another place that keeps this history alive. Near the town of Hazelton, where two rivers meet, the Gitxsan people have a village called Ksan. It's been rebuilt the old way, with big cedar longhouses painted on the front, and tall totem poles standing out front facing the river. The country around the Hazeltons has one of the great collections of standing totem poles anywhere in the world, many of them still in the villages where they were raised.

I've stood in front of those poles, and I'll tell you what struck me. Every figure on them means something. A family, a story, a right to a piece of land or a fishing spot on the river. They're not decorations. They're more like a title deed and a history book, carved into one tree.
And that brings me to something else the North does that most people don't know about.

Out on the coast, there's a group of islands called Haida Gwaii, once known as the Queen Charlotte Islands. They sit way out in the Pacific, off the northern coast of B.C. And right off their western shore runs a giant fault line, where two pieces of the earth's crust grind past each other.

In October of twenty-twelve, that fault slipped. The result was a magnitude seven point eight earthquake, one of the most powerful ever recorded in Canada. It shook the islands hard, it sent a tsunami across the ocean, and waves reached as far as Hawaii. And something else happened, which nobody expected. Some hot springs on the islands, that people had used for generations, stopped flowing for a time after the quake. Just like that, the earth turned off the tap.

Haida Gwaii is one of the most remarkable places I've ever seen. The Haida people have lived there for thousands of years, and on a small island in the south called SGang Gwaay, there's an old village site where tall carved cedar poles still stand, weathered grey and leaning, looking out at the sea. It's a World Heritage Site now. The Haida chose to let those poles return to the earth naturally, rather than lock them in a museum. Standing among them in the mist, with the ocean behind you and moss on everything, you feel like you've stepped back in time.

And the islands have their own wildlife secrets too. Because they're isolated, some animals there developed a little differently from the mainland. The black bears on Haida Gwaii are generally bigger, with larger jaws. Scientists have long studied these islands for exactly that reason. The isolation turned them into a kind of natural laboratory.
But the most famous tree on Haida Gwaii isn't standing anymore, and its story still makes me sad.

On the banks of the Yakoun River, on the main island, there was a giant Sitka spruce, hundreds of years old, unlike any other tree in the world. Its needles weren't green. They were gold. The whole tree glowed yellow in the sun, standing out from the dark forest around it like a candle. Scientists said it was a rare genetic quirk. To the Haida, it was much more than that. They called it K'iid K'iyaas, and it was part of their oral history, a sacred tree tied to a story about a boy who was turned into a tree.

In January of nineteen ninety-seven, a man came to the river at night with a chainsaw. He was a former forestry worker who had turned against the logging industry, and he wanted to make a statement. He cut deep into the trunk, and a few days later, in a winter storm, the Golden Spruce fell.

The whole island was heartbroken. People gathered and mourned it like a funeral. And the man who did it was charged, but he never made it to court. He set out across the stormy water toward the islands in a kayak, and he disappeared. Pieces of his kayak were found later. He never was.

There's a little bit of a happy ending. Cuttings had been taken from the tree, and some of them have been grown into young golden spruces. So somewhere, the gold is still growing. But the old giant on the riverbank is gone.
Let's come back to the mainland now, to a town on the north coast called Prince Rupert.

Most Canadians, if they know Prince Rupert at all, think of it as a rainy fishing town at the end of the highway. And it is rainy. It's one of the wettest towns in Canada. But here's what most people don't know. Prince Rupert has one of the deepest natural harbours in North America, and it doesn't freeze. And even more important, it's the closest major port in North America to Asia. Ships sailing from Prince Rupert to China or Japan save a lot of time compared to ports further south.

That's why, over the last couple of decades, this little town has turned into a big gateway for trade. Trains loaded with containers roll in and out, carrying goods between Asia and the middle of North America. A shipping container can arrive from Shanghai, get loaded onto a train in Prince Rupert, and be in Chicago days later. So when you buy something in a store somewhere in the middle of the continent, there's a chance it came through this foggy, rainy town that most Canadians have never seen.
And here's the thing. Prince Rupert was supposed to be much, much bigger than it is. It was supposed to be the next Vancouver.

Back at the start of the nineteen hundreds, a railway company called the Grand Trunk Pacific wanted to build a new line across Canada, all the way to the Pacific. And the man running it, an American railway boss named Charles Melville Hays, picked this spot on the north coast as the end of the line. He planned a grand city. Wide streets, a big hotel, a great port. They even held a contest to name the town, and Prince Rupert was the winner.

In the spring of nineteen twelve, Hays was in Europe, raising money for his railway. And he booked passage home on a brand new ship, to be back in time for the opening of a grand new hotel. The ship was the Titanic.

Charles Melville Hays went down with it in April of nineteen twelve. And many people say a lot of Prince Rupert's dream went down with him. The railway was finished a couple of years later, but the company went broke, the big plans were scaled back, and Prince Rupert stayed a small town on a rainy harbour, while Vancouver took off.
So in a way, the container trains rolling into Prince Rupert today are finally finishing a dream that started more than a hundred years ago, and sank in the North Atlantic.
Now head inland from the coast, up a long inlet, and you'll find something that I think is one of the most impressive engineering feats in Canadian history. And again, almost nobody knows about it.

In the early nineteen-fifties, an aluminum company wanted to build a giant smelter on the coast, at a place called Kitimat. Aluminum smelting uses huge amounts of electricity. So they needed a power source. And what they did was incredible.

East of the Coast Mountains, there's a system of lakes and rivers that naturally drained east, into the Nechako River, and eventually all the way to the Fraser. The company built a dam that held back that water and turned that chain of lakes into a big reservoir. Then they drilled a tunnel, about sixteen kilometres long, straight through a mountain range, so the water would flow the other way, west, toward the Pacific. At the end of that tunnel, they built a powerhouse. And they didn't build it on the surface. They built it inside the mountain. A huge cave, carved out of solid rock, deep underground, filled with giant generators.

So think about what that means. They took water that had been flowing one way for thousands of years, and sent it backwards, through the heart of a mountain, to make electricity in a cave. That's the Kemano project. And the town of Kitimat, a planned town built from scratch in the wilderness, grew up around the smelter it powered.

But like so much up here, it came with a cost. Turning that water around flooded land that First Nations, like the Cheslatta Carrier, had lived on for generations. Some families were given very little notice before the water came. And the Nechako River, downstream from the dam, has had less water ever since, which has affected the salmon that people rely on. These are stories that the people up there remember well, even if the rest of the country has forgotten.
Let's go north again now, to the very top corner of the province. And this is where things get really remote.

In the far northwest corner of B.C., where it touches Alaska and the Yukon, there's a park called Tatshenshini-Alsek. It's part of the largest protected area of its kind in the world, when you add the parks across the borders in Alaska and the Yukon. Glaciers, icefields, mountains that disappear into the clouds. It's a World Heritage Site.

And in nineteen ninety-nine, some hunters walking near the edge of a melting glacier up there found something incredible. The remains of a young man, preserved in the ice. With him were a walking stick, a hat woven from plant fibres, a fur robe, and some tools. Scientists worked together with the local First Nations, the Champagne and Aishihik people, who gave him a name, Kwäday Dän Ts'ìnchi, which means Long Ago Person Found. He had lived a couple of hundred years ago or more. And because of careful work, including DNA tests with the permission of the community, they even found living people in the region who are related to him.

Think about that. A young man walked out across a glacier centuries ago, and never came home. And the ice kept him, safe and silent, until the climate warmed enough to give him back. Up there, the land doesn't just hide things. It keeps them.
And speaking of the border, there's one more little secret along that line that always makes people laugh when I tell it.

On the coast, at the head of a long canal, there's a small town called Stewart, British Columbia. And right next door, just a couple of kilometres away, is a tiny place called Hyder, Alaska. It's one of the only places where you can drive into Alaska from Canada without going through American customs at all. There's no U.S. border post. You just drive across. Coming back into Canada, though, you do have to stop at the Canadian booth. Hyder is so cut off from the rest of Alaska that for years it used Canadian money, Canadian phone codes, and it runs on Canadian time.

And just up the road from there, you can drive to the Salmon Glacier, one of the biggest glaciers in the world that you can actually reach by road. You stand up on the ridge and look down, and the glacier spreads out below you like a frozen highway, blue and white, winding between the peaks. I've brought visitors there who just stood there with their mouths open and didn't say a word for five minutes.
Before we go, I want to tell you about one more thing. Because for me, it's the heart of what makes the North different.

Just south of the Alaska Highway, and along the coast, there's a kind of land that doesn't look like anywhere else in Canada. Mountains that drop straight into the sea. Rainforests where the trees are so big and so old that five people holding hands couldn't reach around them. Rivers so full of salmon in the fall that you could almost walk across their backs.

And in those coastal rainforests lives a bear that most people think is a legend. It's a black bear, but it's white. Not an albino. A real black bear with a creamy white coat, caused by a rare gene. The Kermode bear. The spirit bear. The Indigenous people of the coast have told stories about it for countless generations. On a few islands out there, a surprising number of the black bears carry that white coat. And seeing one, standing in a river in the green rainforest, glowing almost like a ghost, is something you don't forget.

I saw one once, from a float plane, years ago. Just a flash of white on a river bank, and then it was gone into the trees. I circled back three times and never saw it again. Some days I wonder if I imagined it. But I know I didn't.
And I'll leave you with one last place, because it's where a lot of this story really began.

In the middle of the province, on the shore of Stuart Lake, there's a town called Fort St. James. In eighteen-oh-six, a fur trader named Simon Fraser came through this country and set up a trading post there. It became one of the oldest places in British Columbia that has been lived in continuously by people of European background. For more than a century, it was the centre of the fur trade for this whole northern region, a place the traders called New Caledonia.

The Dakelh people, the Carrier, had lived around that lake for thousands of years, and they were the ones who knew how to survive in this country. They traded furs, salmon, and knowledge. The traders brought in iron tools, blankets, and goods from the other side of the world. And for good and for bad, the North that we know today started to take shape around posts like this one.

Today you can visit Fort St. James and walk through the old trading post buildings, restored to the way they looked around a hundred years ago. The fur warehouse, the fish cache, the officers' house. They even have people dressed in period clothing who'll tell you how it all worked. I stood in that old fur warehouse once, with the smell of the wood and the sound of the lake outside, and thought about all the canoes that had pulled up on that beach over the centuries. It's one of the few places in the North where you can actually feel the past standing right next to you.

So that's northern British Columbia. A land where towns are built and then vanish. Where volcanoes have buried villages within the last few centuries. Where rivers have been turned around and sent through mountains. Where the ice gives back people who walked out onto it long ago. Where an American road built in eight months during the war still winds through the wilderness. And where the animals still outnumber the people by a very long way.

Most Canadians will never go up there. And maybe that's part of what keeps it the way it is. But I think everybody in this country should at least know it's there. Because the North isn't empty. It's full. Full of stories, full of history, full of things we've forgotten and things we never knew.

I've spent my whole life flying over that country, and I'm still finding things that surprise me. If you enjoyed this trip, stick around, because next time we're heading out to Vancouver Island. And trust me, there's a lot more going on out there than most people think.
Take care of yourselves. I'm Gordie, and I'll see you up the road.
